item.title: Nancy Guthrie investigators see uptick in tips after ransom notes release: Sheriff
item.description: The Pima County Sheriff's Office reports a slight increase in tips after releasing two purported ransom notes sent to Nancy Guthrie's family.
item.content:encoded:
Authorities have seen an increase in tips after releasing the ransom notes that were sent to Nancy Guthrie's family.

Authorities have not confirmed the ransom notes are authentic, but their release has generated a "slight" uptick in tips, a spokeswoman for the Pima County Sheriff's Office said. The office released the full content of the alleged notes on July 31.

"Nancy Guthrie Task Force investigators have seen a slight increase in tips since the two ransom notes were released last week," Pima County Sheriff's Office Public Information Officer Angelica Carrillo told Fox News Digital. "All tips have been followed up on."

NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM DEMANDS RELEASED BY PIMA COUNTY SHERIFF'S DEPARTMENT IN BID TO IDENTIFY SENDER

The alleged ransom notes were sent on Feb. 2 and Feb. 6.

"Hello Savannah," one of the notes read. "We have your mother Nancy. She is safe but scared. She will be held for ransom and once payment is received she will be released unharmed."

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"She had a white smart watch on the floor of the foot of her bed and the white flood light in backyard was destroyed," it continued.

In a follow-up message sent to the Guthrie family, the alleged ransom notes states that Nancy Guthrie has passed away.

"We did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition. We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention. She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart related," the purported ransom note states.

As previously noted, Fox News Digital has not independently verified the authenticity of the notes or their contents.

Jason Pack, a retired FBI negotiator, said the watch detail demonstrates familiarity with the house but not necessarily knowledge unique to Guthrie or proof that she was alive.

"He knew about the watch on the floor — almost nobody did," Pack said. "In my view, two things the language does support: He writes like a native English speaker. The idiom and the small connecting words are all in the right places, and at this length that is hard to fake."

item.title: 'Melrose Place' star Andrew Shue says 70% believe the American Dream is 'dead or dying'
item.description: Andrew Shue claims 70% of Americans believe the American dream is dead or dying, driving him to launch The Forum bipartisan civic initiative.
item.content:encoded:
Former "Melrose Place" star Andrew Shue believes that the majority of Americans have lost faith in the promise that once defined the country.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, the 59-year-old actor, who founded the new bipartisan initiative The Forum, shared his grim assessment of the current mood of citizens in the United States, arguing that people across the economic and political spectrum are struggling.

JOHN ADAMS MADE A TERRIFYING PREDICTION. AMERICA IS CLOSE TO PROVING HIM CORRECT

"There's nobody in this country right now that thinks we're in a good place," Shue said. "You look around and you say, how do we feel about our kids? How do we fill it feel about our kid's future? What kind of anxiety level do we all have? You're seeing 70% believe the American dream is dead or dying."

"So we're all in this boat together," he continued. "There's nobody who's jumping out, whether you're a billionaire, a bartender, everybody in between, we are all in this together."

Shue said that Americans' growing pessimism is not being driven by a single election or political figure, but by systemic problems he believes have accumulated over decades.

"We're realizing that the engine is broken and the main systems that drive that engine are our political system and our economic system," Shue explained. "The political system only rewards people in power — there happen to be a lot of old people — and performative conflict. The economic system is really just rewarding people at the top. Ninety percent feel like they're treading water or underwater, and have been for decades. The other thing I'll say is all of these problems existed long before [current U.S. President] Donald Trump came to the scene."

WATCH HERE: ‘MELROSE PLACE’ ALUM ANDREW SHUE SAYS 70% BELIEVE THE AMERICAN DREAM IS ‘DEAD OR DYING’

WORLD SERIES CHAMPION JOE GIRARDI REVEALS WHAT HE FINDS MOST 'DISTURBING' ABOUT POLITICS TODAY

"And so, as we look around, and we're fighting each other, and we try to figure out, what are we gonna do? Who's coming to save us? The answer is right in front of us," he continued. "It's us. It's the American people. The question is, ‘Oh, that seems kind of obvious. Yeah, the consent of the governed.’ We are the ones who are supposed to be the ultimate authority."

To help address what he sees as the country's growing divide, Shue founded The Forum, a nonpartisan civic initiative that brings together politically diverse Americans to identify areas of agreement and develop policy proposals. The initiative has already been implemented in three early primary states, including South Carolina, New Hampshire and Nevada.

"We have launched the Forum that I've been working on for the last eight years with an incredible team," he said. "It's the place and the process for the American people to co-create that renewal agenda. Over 300,000 people have participated so far. Perfectly politically balanced — conservatives showing up, liberals showing up, people on the far left, far right — everybody's showing up, and we have credibility and legitimacy."

"Elected leaders from both sides who put down their arms are actually leading the efforts in each state," he added. "So this is the way forward. The question is, will the legislators, the elected leaders, follow? The American people are ready to lead."

SEN CHUCK SCHUMER UNVEILS ANTI-CORRUPTION AGENCY AIMED AT TRUMP AND FUTURE PRESIDENTS

As the initiative has expanded across three states, Shue told Fox News Digital that he has been struck by how quickly participants find common ground despite their political differences.

"I think that the thing that surprised me the most was that when you give people this assignment, you say, 'It's now on you, you are going to be the hero of the story. All you have to do is work together, listen to each other, listen to your lived experiences, and come up with something that you can agree on,'" Shue said.

WATCH HERE: ‘MELROSE PLACE’ ALUM ANDREW SHUE LAUNCHES NEW BIPARTISAN INITIATIVE THE FORUM TO BREAK AMERICA'S POLITICAL GRIDLOCK

"And 70% have to agree — that's the supermajority number, 70% or higher — and then it can go forward as draft legislation," he continued. "And the thing that's beautiful is when you get these people in the rooms with people who are different, they can't figure out who the Democrat or the Republican is. They see all the common values. They see the common goal."

"Once you start listening to each other, once you start feeling like you're on the same team, and you have the same goal, anything's possible," Shue added. "And people are desperate. That's the thing. People are desperate. They're really ready for something new."

AS AMERICA MARKS 250 YEARS, OUR GREATEST CHAPTERS ARE STILL AHEAD OF US

The Delaware native also reflected on what has restored his optimism about Americans and what they can achieve when they are united.

"That we know what makes America, America," he said. "It's about that confidence, that belief in what's possible. You know, I think [U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it best, 'Anyone from anywhere can become anything.' And people believe that and they live that."

"America is a place — obviously we talk about opportunity — it's a place that gives everybody a shot," Shue continued. "And this is the moment where, again, we talk about the hero. This is the moment for the American people to be the heroes."

While Shue has largely stepped away from Hollywood, he said his "Melrose Place" fame has helped shine a spotlight on The Forum.

"It certainly hasn't hurt," he said. "People are a little bit confused. And then I tell them what I've been doing for the last eight years and how committed I've been to this project."

"This provides not just the pathway to create that renewal agenda, not just a pathway to create this new power source that's going to kind of break through this partisan gridlock that we have, but it's the opportunity for everybody to be part of something," Shue explained.

WATCH HERE: ANDREW SHUE CALLS ‘MELROSE’ PLACE THE ‘ULTIMATE EXAMPLE OF THE AMERICAN DREAM’

"If you think about even MAGA and you say, why was MAGA so strong? It's because they belonged to something," he added. "But we need to belong to something that's not about beating the other side. We've got to belong to something that's about going somewhere together. We want to be on the same team. We are so exhausted with our politics."

"The American people can do this, create that renewal agenda, and then we create the power base to enforce it. And like I said, the elected leaders are going to have to go along with it because this is the only way we can do it."

Reflecting on the personal challenges he has faced in recent years, Shue said difficult experiences have changed the way he approaches relationships and community.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"It definitely makes you try to put yourself in other people's shoes," he said. "To walk in other people's shoes is such an important part of building any kind of community, building any kind of understanding. We are all flawed. We are trying to be better people. We make decisions sometimes that don't work out for us or for our kids."

"And those experiences, when you really struggle, and you go through something painful, it teaches you what you're all about," Shue added.

As Shue now spends his time trying to help others rediscover faith in the American Dream, he said that he feels he experienced it firsthand during his own acting career when he landed his starring role on "Melrose Place."

MICRON'S $250 MILLION BET ON KIDS IS A BLUEPRINT FOR AMERICA'S FUTURE

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"It just gave me a ton of confidence," he said. "It gave me doors that were opened and it gave me a platform. And it came at a time in my life where I was a little bit trying to figure out my direction and what I was capable of. But it did give me possibility. I mean, it was the ultimate example of the American dream."

"It was a real boost to my confidence and a boost to my thought process about what could be possible."

item.title: READ THE DOCUMENTS: Secret ‘Oxferd Comma’ probe cast Trump as potential Russian asset after Comey firing
item.description: The FBI opened a counterintelligence probe codenamed "Oxferd Comma" after Trump fired James Comey, seeking direct ties to the Russian Federation.
item.content:encoded:
The White House released a trove of documents showing that the FBI opened a 2017 investigation into whether President Donald Trump was acting on behalf of or under the influence of Russia when he fired FBI Director James Comey.

The investigation, codenamed "Oxferd Comma," opened after Trump fired Comey in May 2017, according to the White House’s release. 

Investigators sought to determine whether Trump was "directed by, controlled by, and/or coordinated activities with, the Russian Federation in a manner constituting a threat to the national security of the United States and/or a violation of federal criminal statutes," according to an FBI memo dated May 16, 2017. The memo also said investigators would examine whether Trump or others had obstructed or conspired to obstruct an associated FBI investigation.

TRUMP ALLY DIGENOVA TAPPED TO LEAD DOJ PROBE INTO BRENNAN OVER RUSSIA PROBE ORIGINS

The opening memo cited information developed during Crossfire Hurricane, the FBI’s counterintelligence investigation into whether individuals associated with Trump’s 2016 campaign were coordinating with the Russian government to interfere in the 2016 election.

READ THE DOCUMENTS:

It also identified later events and information, including Trump’s interactions with Comey, the administration’s shifting explanations for Comey’s firing, Trump campaign discussions concerning the Republican platform’s language on Ukraine aid and Trump’s business ties and real estate interests involving Russia.

SECRET FBI PROBE CAST TRUMP AS POSSIBLE RUSSIAN ASSET AFTER COMEY FIRING, MEMOS SHOW

Trump initially cited Comey’s handling of the FBI investigation into Hillary Clinton’s use of a private email server while she was secretary of state as the reason for his ouster, though he later said the Russia investigation was also on his mind when he made the decision.

The FBI memo said the circumstances surrounding Comey’s dismissal could support an inference that the bureau’s counterintelligence investigation was a factor in Trump’s decision to fire Comey.

READ THE DOCUMENTS:

However, the decision to open the investigation did not mean those suspicions had been substantiated.

Special counsel Robert Mueller, appointed in 2017 to investigate Russian election interference, reported in 2019 that his team did not establish coordination between the Trump campaign and Russia and did not make a prosecutorial decision on obstruction. Attorney General William Barr appointed John Durham to review the origins and handling of the FBI’s Russia investigation in 2019. Durham’s 2023 report concluded that the FBI opened the full Crossfire Hurricane investigation without sufficient evidentiary support and did not apply the same rigor it had used in other sensitive investigations.

READ THE DOCUMENTS:

A separate 2019 Justice Department inspector general review found the FBI had enough information under its rules to open Crossfire Hurricane, though it later identified serious errors and omissions in surveillance applications involving former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page.

A review of the White House’s original release shows the code name rendered as "Oxferd Comma," with the letter "o." Former acting Assistant Attorney General Jeff Clark, who served in Trump’s first administration, said a document expert he consulted concluded the "o" in "Comma" found within the FBI documents was a zero. Clark speculated the unusual spelling was intended to make the records harder to find through FOIA searches.

The documents were published by the White House Wednesday, which said they had been declassified and released through its Government Transparency Task Force.

item.title: Senate Republicans push Election Day deadline for California's marathon ballot counts
item.description: Sens. James Lankford and Mike Lee cite a Supreme Court ruling as they push legislation requiring all mail-in ballots be received by the time polls close.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: A pair of Senate Republicans are bursting through a crack in the door left by the Supreme Court to force blue states like California to vastly cut down on how long it takes to count ballots.

Sens. James Lankford, R-Okla., and Mike Lee, R-Utah, are introducing legislation that would create a federal deadline for states to accept ballots received by the time polls close on Election Day across the country.

Lankford pitched the bill, called the Ballots by Election Day Act, as a bid to build more trust in the country’s elections.

TRUMP UNLOADS AFTER SUPREME COURT UPHOLDS LATE MAIL-IN BALLOTS IN MISSISSIPPI

"I have made fun of other states for years because there's quite a few states around the country that can't seem to figure out how to be able to count," Lankford told Fox News Digital in an interview. "In Oklahoma, our election ends at 7 p.m. on a Tuesday night."

"Usually by 9 p.m., all of our thousands of precincts are all in and counted," he continued. "We start the verification process. We do an audit after that. We have great trust in our elections because we know. We all vote. But we get them all in on that."

Lankford and Lee’s bill would create a nationwide deadline for counting absentee and mail-in ballots, meaning that if those ballots aren’t in by the time polls close across the expanse of time zones in the nation, they won’t be counted.

CALIFORNIA’S SLUGGISH VOTE COUNTING RIPPED ACROSS THE POLITICAL SPECTRUM: 'EXTREMELY EMBARRASSING'

It targets states, like California and Washington state, where ballot counting can take days, sometimes weeks, beyond when polls close.

"States counting late ballots are inviting fraud and sowing doubt in their own election results," Lee told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Our bill will clarify protocol and restore trust by counting only ballots received before the polls close on Election Day."

Lankford contended that those states, "like California and others, New York," breed distrust in the system.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP'S ELECTION ORDER AS SAVE AMERICA ACT FIGHT INTENSIFIES

"When you vote you may not know for weeks to months what the final election count is," he said. "That shouldn't be in the United States of America."

Their push comes after the Supreme Court’s decision to allow mail-in ballots post-marked before Election Day to still be counted if they came in later.

While the court contended that mail-in balloting could continue, it didn’t explicitly address that there could be no deadline for when the ballots could be counted.

"Once the court made their ruling, as that came out, they left a clear door open to say this could be defined by the United States Congress," Lankford said. "So I said, let's step in and actually do that. Let us provide some real clarity for that. This shouldn't be controversial. This should just be something to build trust in our elections."

item.title: Iran is moving its tanks. Decades as a military planner taught me what that means
item.description: Iran's 92nd Armored Division reportedly moved T-72 tanks toward Abadan even as diplomacy over the Strait of Hormuz and nuclear program advances.
item.content:encoded:
During nearly five decades in uniform and as a Pentagon strategist, I served alongside armored and mechanized forces in South Korea, at Fort Riley and in divided Cold War Germany. While stationed along the Iron Curtain, I helped plan the defense against a Soviet armor-heavy assault through the Fulda Gap and across NATO's central front. Later, during the Iraq War, I observed firsthand how American armored formations were employed in combat.

One lesson stayed with me.

Military professionals rarely begin by asking what politicians are saying. They begin by asking what armies are doing.

TRUMP MAY CLAIM HE WON THE FIGHT WITH IRAN, BUT THERE’S A BIGGER WAR ALREADY UNDERWAY

Professional soldiers are trained to see what others overlook. Not necessarily because they possess better information, but because they ask different questions.

Politicians communicate through speeches. Diplomats communicate through negotiations. Armies reveal themselves through force posture. A brigade quietly changes location. Engineers strengthen defensive positions. Fuel and ammunition move forward. Reserve formations reposition. None of those actions guarantee war, but together they often reveal something more valuable than public statements: what commanders believe may happen next.

US EYES FIRST-EVER HYPERSONIC DARK EAGLE DEPLOYMENT AS IRAN PUSHES BEYOND STRIKE RANGE

Throughout my career, I learned that tanks rarely tell you who is about to attack. They tell you what commanders think is coming.

That is why recent reports deserve careful attention. Elements reportedly associated with Iran's 92nd Armored Division moved T-72 tanks toward the southern approaches near Abadan on August 1. If confirmed, the movement matters, not because it proves an American ground campaign is imminent, but because it may reveal what Iranian planners are preparing to confront.

Professional militaries do not reposition conventional formations casually. Armor consumes enormous amounts of fuel and logistical support. Commanders accept those costs only when the movement serves a real operational purpose.

Whether Tehran ultimately employs those forces is almost beside the point.

The more important question is this: What does Iran believe may come next?

WEAPONS STOCKPILE SHORTAGES IMPACTING MILITARY STRATEGY IN THE MIDEAST

This distinction reflects the difference between military intelligence and operational planning. Intelligence assesses capabilities and intentions. Planners then translate that into a harder question: What mission does the adversary appear to be preparing to execute?

Force posture often reveals expectations more clearly than official statements, because governments can disguise intentions more easily than they can disguise preparations.

Armies rarely announce what they expect. They quietly organize for it.

The reported movement deserves attention precisely because it involves the Artesh rather than the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Americans understandably focus on the IRGC. It oversees Iran's missiles, drones, proxy forces and the security of the Islamic regime. The Artesh serves another purpose entirely. It is Iran's conventional army, organized principally to defend Iranian territory against external attack.

Military organizations reposition forces for many reasons: dispersing vulnerable assets, conducting an exercise, strengthening deterrence, signaling political resolve, or preparing for a changing mission. The planner's task is to determine which explanation best fits the broader pattern of events.

WHO IS AHMAD VAHIDI? IRAN’S NEW IRGC CHIEF TIED TO GLOBAL ATTACKS AND ‘DEATH TO AMERICA’ IDEOLOGY

In this case, if accurate, the more plausible explanation is not an offensive against neighboring states, but preparation for a fight that evolves beyond today's exchange of missiles, drones and airstrikes into one over Iranian territory itself.

That observation should not be misunderstood. It does not predict an American invasion of Iran.

Professional militaries prepare for possibilities long before political leaders decide whether those possibilities become policy. Military planning is an exercise in managing uncertainty. Good commanders prepare for futures they hope never occur, because hope has never been a planning assumption.

History repeatedly demonstrates why force posture deserves careful study. During the Cold War, NATO intelligence officers watched Warsaw Pact armored deployments almost continuously. Tanks alone never revealed Soviet intentions. Supporting engineers, logistics, artillery, bridging equipment and reserve movements often proved far more revealing.

Experienced planners learned to read military behavior the way physicians read symptoms: not as isolated facts, but as evidence of a larger condition. The task was spotting convergence, not isolated movement.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN WILL BE HIT 'REALLY HARD' IF NUCLEAR NEGOTIATIONS COLLAPSE AGAIN

The same lesson emerged when Saddam Hussein invaded Iran in September 1980. Saddam mistook revolutionary turmoil and military disorganization for strategic weakness. He expected a rapid victory. Instead, Iran reorganized, mobilized and transformed what Baghdad expected would be a short campaign into an exhausting eight-year war. Saddam confused visible weakness with imminent collapse, a mistake strategists should not repeat when assessing Iran today.

Many observers now assume the war in Ukraine demonstrated that tanks are obsolete. It demonstrated something more nuanced. Tanks operating without infantry, engineers, electronic warfare, air defense and drones become exceptionally vulnerable.

Yet tanks remain indispensable because armies still require protected mobility, mobile firepower and the ability to seize and hold terrain. Technology has changed how tanks fight. It has not changed why armies still need them.

ARMY IDS 2 VICTIMS KILLED IN JORDAN AIR BASE ATTACK; TRUMP: IRAN WILL PAY 'MANY TIMES OVER'

Iranian doctrine reflects the same reality. Its armored formations are not meant to defeat American forces tank for tank. They can reinforce corridors, support infantry, protect critical sites and complicate any attempt to seize terrain or expand a ground presence. Integrated with difficult terrain, prepared positions, mines and air defense, even aging armor can delay, disrupt and raise the cost of escalation.

Ironically, these reported military preparations come as diplomacy appears to be gaining momentum. Oman-mediated contacts between the United States and Iran have reportedly made progress toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz while creating an opportunity for broader discussions over Iran's nuclear program.

To many civilians, those developments appear contradictory.

Professional soldiers see them differently.

Experienced planners expect governments to negotiate while armies continue preparing for the possibility that negotiations fail. That is not cynicism; it is prudence. Military organizations exist to preserve options for political leaders should diplomacy falter, not because they expect war, but because they cannot afford to be surprised by it.

IRAN WAR'S PRICE TAG HITS $80B — MORE THAN DOUBLE WHAT CONGRESS WAS TOLD

That reality now confronts President Donald Trump. Military pressure appears to have created genuine diplomatic leverage. His challenge is converting that pressure into verifiable results, freedom of navigation through Hormuz, enforceable constraints on Iran's nuclear program and greater regional stability, before demands expand into objectives airpower alone cannot deliver.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

History suggests the hardest strategic decision is not when to begin military operations, but when additional destruction stops producing proportionate political gain.

Throughout my Army career, I learned that armies tip their hand long before they fight, not through speeches or press conferences, but through logistics, doctrine, training and force posture. Tanks are simply one part of that larger language.

Iran's aging armored vehicles may never fire a shot in this conflict. In fact, the tanks themselves are almost incidental. What matters is what their reported movement suggests about how Tehran may be thinking.

A strategist's first responsibility is not merely to prepare for the next battle, but to recognize when an adversary's preparations create an opportunity to prevent it. Reading force posture correctly is not simply about predicting war. At its best, it gives statesmen the understanding necessary to preserve peace before military expectations harden into military necessity.

item.title: Russian hackers can steal emails without a click
item.description: Laundry Bear exploits security flaw in unpatched Zimbra servers, stealing 90 days of emails and authentication data without victims clicking a link.
item.content:encoded:
Opening an unexpected email can feel relatively harmless when you avoid its links and attachments. However, a Russian hacking campaign has turned that familiar safety advice on its head.

CISA says the Russian state-sponsored group Laundry Bear can compromise certain email accounts when someone simply opens or previews a malicious message. The attack targets organizations running unpatched versions of the Zimbra Collaboration Suite.

Once the email appears, hidden code can collect passwords, authentication data and as much as 90 days of messages. You may never see a warning or realize that anything happened.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued the warning with the National Security Agency, FBI and cyber authorities from several allied countries. The agencies say the group has successfully targeted more than 10 Western organizations since July 2025.

INVESTIGATORS BELIEVE IRANIAN HACKERS ARE LIKELY BEHIND CYBERATTACK ON MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEMS: REPORT

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

Laundry Bear, which Microsoft tracks as Void Blizzard, exploits a security flaw known as CVE-2025-66376. The cross-site scripting vulnerability affects the Classic user interface in certain versions of the Zimbra Collaboration Suite.

Zimbra is an email and collaboration platform used by some governments, schools, businesses and other organizations as an alternative to services such as Microsoft Exchange or Google Workspace. Attackers can place malicious JavaScript inside a specially crafted HTML email. That code runs automatically when a vulnerable Zimbra webmail client displays the message.

The person reading the email does not need to open an attachment. The attack also avoids the usual request to enter a password on an obvious phishing page. However, the email still needs to appear on the screen. CISA describes the technique as a zero-click exploit. Proofpoint calls it a "half-click" attack because someone must open the email or allow it to appear in a preview pane. Either description leads to the same concern. A message can look harmless while code hidden inside it quietly attacks the email account.

Laundry Bear reportedly used the flaw as a zero-day before Zimbra released a patch in November 2025. A zero-day attack exploits a security weakness before the software maker provides a fix. CISA later added the vulnerability to its list of flaws that hackers actively exploit.

The available patch closes the known security hole. Yet Laundry Bear continues to target organizations that have not installed the update. That makes delayed patching especially dangerous. An organization may have strong passwords and trained employees, but an exposed email server can still give attackers another way inside.

The campaign has reached organizations connected to the defense industrial base and government. Attackers have also targeted education, energy, law enforcement, media, nonprofit groups and technology companies.

According to CISA, the malicious code attempts to collect the target's last 90 days of email. That could include private conversations with coworkers, contract discussions or information about upcoming meetings. An inbox may also contain password reset notices, invoices and documents that reveal how an organization operates.

Laundry Bear also collects the person's email address and password. The attack can copy the organization's Global Address List, which acts as a directory of employees and contacts. The hackers may then gain enough information to impersonate a trusted coworker or identify more valuable accounts.

CISA says the exploit also targets two-factor authentication tokens. Those tokens help prove that someone has already completed an authentication step. A stolen token or session cookie can let an attacker enter an account without completing the normal login process again.

FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK

Stealing information provides immediate value, but Laundry Bear also tries to preserve its access. The attack creates a new Zimbra application passcode and sends it back to the hackers. Legacy email programs use these passcodes when they connect through services such as IMAP or ActiveSync and cannot support modern time-based authentication.

An unauthorized passcode can give the hackers another entrance to the mailbox. That access may continue even after someone changes the main account password. CISA has urged administrators to look for suspicious application passcodes, particularly passcodes labeled "ZimbraWeb."

Organizations should treat an unknown passcode as a sign that someone may have entered the account. Simply installing the patch after a compromise may leave the attacker's access in place.

Laundry Bear sends the stolen information to servers controlled by the group. CISA says the attackers use a collection framework called Flowerbed. The system moves smaller pieces of data through Domain Name System requests. DNS normally helps computers find websites and online services.

Attackers can hide encoded information inside those requests. Because organizations generate large amounts of legitimate DNS traffic, the malicious activity may blend into the background. Laundry Bear sends larger collections through encrypted HTTPS connections. That can include compressed archives containing mailbox data. Security teams may need to inspect network logs, authentication records and mailbox activity to understand what left the organization.

Laundry Bear also uses adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits. These tools create login pages that closely resemble legitimate email portals. When someone enters a username and password, the phishing system captures those credentials. It can also intercept session cookies created during the login process. That means an attacker may gain access even when the account uses conventional multifactor authentication.

CISA's indicators of compromise include domains that impersonated Zimbra infrastructure. Examples include mailnalysis.com, zimbrastat.com, zimbra-metadata.com and zmailanalytics.com. The presence of one of these domains in network logs could point to phishing or unauthorized account activity. However, organizations should review CISA's complete list because attackers can change their infrastructure.

Proofpoint found that Laundry Bear sent messages from attacker-controlled Proton Mail accounts and email addresses the group had already compromised. In one example, the sender claimed to represent a Belgian media-verification organization. The email proposed cooperation between European institutions fighting disinformation. It included a legitimate-looking link to a European Union events calendar. However, the malicious code sat inside the email rather than the linked website.

Dutch intelligence agencies publicly identified Laundry Bear in May 2025. Their investigation linked the group to a 2024 breach of the Dutch National Police. That incident exposed personal information belonging to police personnel. Investigators said the attack helped them identify a previously unknown Russian cyberespionage group.

Since at least 2024, Laundry Bear has focused on organizations connected to Russian strategic interests. Its targets have included NATO member states and groups supporting Ukraine.

Microsoft has documented compromises involving defense organizations as well as entities in transportation and aviation.A separate campaign targeted members of Ukraine's military with charity-themed phishing emails. Those messages disguised malware as requests for donations.

These campaigns suggest the group cares more about long-term intelligence collection than a quick financial payout. Access to email can reveal relationships, future plans and internal decisions.

PAIDWORK BREACH EXPOSES 23M USER RECORDS

The strongest protection starts with the organization running the email server because employees cannot personally patch a vulnerable installation. However, you can still take steps to spot suspicious activity and protect your other accounts.

Administrators should update Zimbra Collaboration Suite to a currently supported version and install all available security fixes. Organizations should confirm that the patch reached every server. An overlooked system may remain exposed even when the primary mail server has received the update.

Installing the patch blocks the known flaw, but it cannot undo a previous intrusion. Security teams should review CISA's published indicators of compromise. They should also search network records for connections to the listed domains and IP addresses. Authentication logs may reveal unusual locations, unexpected devices or activity outside normal working hours.

Review every Zimbra application passcode connected to an account. Pay close attention to unfamiliar entries and anything labeled "ZimbraWeb." Revoke any passcode that the account owner or IT department cannot verify. Because application passcodes can survive a regular password change, this review plays an important role in removing persistent access.

Administrators should examine mailbox access records and forwarding settings. They should also look for unfamiliar filters, deleted messages or sent emails that the account owner does not recognize. A compromised account may send convincing phishing messages to coworkers because the email comes from a trusted internal address.

Contact your IT or security team if you notice unfamiliar sent messages, unexpected password resets or login alerts you cannot explain. Do not rely only on changing your password. Laundry Bear can create an application passcode that may continue providing mailbox access after the main password changes. Your IT team should revoke unauthorized passcodes, end active sessions and check the account for suspicious activity.

Wait until your IT department has patched the server and removed unauthorized access. Then change your email password and any other password you reused. Create a unique password for every account. A password manager can generate strong credentials and store them securely. Hackers may test stolen email credentials on banking, shopping or social media accounts. Reused passwords can turn one compromised inbox into several compromised accounts.

CISA recommends phishing-resistant multifactor authentication where organizations can support it. Security keys and passkeys provide stronger protection than methods that rely on temporary codes. However, organizations still need to patch the underlying email software. Authentication controls cannot fully protect an account when malicious code runs inside a vulnerable webmail interface.

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious downloads, fake login pages and follow-up malware connected to a broader phishing campaign. However, antivirus software may not stop this email exploit because the malicious code runs inside a vulnerable webmail session. Your organization still needs to update Zimbra and investigate the account for unauthorized access. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

An email login page can look convincing and still belong to an attacker. Instead of following a link inside an email, open your organization's known webmail address directly. Report unfamiliar authentication requests or repeated sign-in prompts to your security team. A sudden request to log in again could signal a phishing attempt or unauthorized account activity.

For years, we have warned you to avoid suspicious links and unexpected attachments. That advice still helps, but Laundry Bear shows why your organization also needs to keep the software behind your inbox updated. In this campaign, viewing an email can trigger malicious code on an unpatched server. The attackers can then reach into the mailbox, collect months of messages and steal authentication data. The hidden application passcode adds another concern. Changing a password may provide a false sense of security when an attacker has already created a separate route back into the account. Organizations using Zimbra should patch immediately and then investigate for signs of earlier access. Employees should remain cautious around unexpected login pages, even when the page carries familiar company branding.

Would you trust your workplace inbox if opening one message could expose 90 days of email without you clicking a link? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: GOP senator deals crushing blow to Trump's AG nominee after Alaska lobbying blitz
item.description: Todd Blanche's attorney general confirmation lost its last cushion as Lisa Murkowski cited the Epstein files and the $2 billion anti-weaponization fund.
item.content:encoded:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche just lost the last little bit of cushion he had left to survive confirmation.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, announced that she would not support Blanche’s nomination to be the nation’s top prosecutor and law enforcement official, dealing another blow to his rocky confirmation process.

Her defection, despite a heavy lobbying effort by Blanche that saw him make the trek to Alaska, means that Senate Republican leadership can’t afford to lose anymore votes to get him across the finish line, given that Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., though now back home, has still not returned to the Senate.

COLLINS DROPS THE HAMMER ON TRUMP'S PICK TO LEAD DOJ, JEOPARDIZING PATH TO CONFIRMATION

Murkowski acknowledged Blanche’s visit to Alaska and heavy lobbying effort throughout the last few weeks, but it’s his connection to President Donald Trump’s nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund, and broader concerns of a weaponized Justice Department, that proved the nail in the coffin for her.

"The politicization — even weaponization — of the Department did not start with this administration but has accelerated during it," Murkowski said in a statement. "I take issue with the handling of the release of the Epstein files; the sweeping immunity protections granted to the President, his family, and their businesses; the statements that have been made to anti-abortion groups; and the repeated targeting of individuals ranging from former administration staff to sitting U.S. Senators."

"I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund—which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters—is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage," she continued. "Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds."

TRUMP'S AG PICK SURVIVES — FOR NOW — AS REPUBLICANS QUESTION IF WHITE HOUSE DEAL WILL HOLD

To Murkowski’s latter issue, several lawmakers in both sides of the aisle acknowledge that though Blanche and the Department of Justice (DOJ) agreed to permanently rescind the fund in writing to Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, there’s nothing stopping Trump from reviving it.

And he’s on several occasions made clear he wants to see it come back.

Before making her decision, Trump already took a snipe at her during an interview with Punch Bowl News published Friday morning.

TRUMP THREATENS TO YANK HIS OWN AG NOMINEE AS GOP REVOLT GROWS

"I’m against Murkowski," Trump said. "I do more for Alaska than any president in history. No president’s done for Alaska what I’ve done. She’s not good."

Meanwhile, it’s unclear whether the Senate will actually vote on Blanche on Friday, which could be the upper chamber’s grand finale of the summer before it exits Washington, D.C., for the remainder of August.

And there’s still one more Republican that hasn’t weighed in on how they’ll vote: Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La.

If he defects, and McConnell is still gone, it will be a 50-50 vote. That means Vice President JD Vance would need to break the tie. But for now, only Murkowski and Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, are publicly opposing Blanche’s confirmation.

"The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration," Murkowski said. "I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case."

item.title: Ghostly outline of long-lost garden at Winston Churchill's birthplace revealed in aerial photos
item.description: Aerial photos reveal the outline of a 300-year-old formal garden at Blenheim Palace, Winston Churchill's birthplace, after dry weather created parch marks across the grounds.
item.content:encoded:
Sweltering heat in the United Kingdom has revealed the remains of a long-lost 18th-century garden at a major tourist attraction.

Aerial photos show the outline of the 300-year-old formal garden at Blenheim Palace, an estate about eight miles northwest of Oxford, England, news agency SWNS reported.

Blenheim Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site built between 1705 and 1722, is famously the birthplace of Sir Winston Churchill, as well as the ancestral home of the Dukes of Marlborough.

HIDDEN UNDERGROUND CHAMBER REVEALED BENEATH HOME OF LEGENDARY ROMAN EMPEROR

The outline was revealed during the latest heat wave this summer after prolonged dry weather created parch marks, or dry patches in the grass, across the grounds.

A spokesperson from Blenheim Palace told Fox News Digital the marks will be visible "until cooler temperatures arrive and sufficient rain falls to green up the shallow-rooted grass."

"There isn't currently any rain in the forecast for the next few weeks, so it will be visible for a while yet," the representative added.

The patches, officials say, reveal the outline of the original garden, giving a glimpse of what it looked like 300 years ago.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER SPRAWLING ROMAN ESTATE BURIED FOR CENTURIES BENEATH FARMLAND

It was originally created in 1705 by royal gardener Henry Wise and was once protected by a high stone wall with bastions.

The garden was dismantled in 1760s, SWNS said, when Blenheim Palace's gardener Lancelot "Capability" Brown redesigned the palace grounds.

The technical term for the garden is a "parterre," from the French term par terre, meaning "on the ground."

Pictures show that the parterre consisted of symmetrical flower beds and paths.

item.title: Which teams are overrated or underrated in new preseason college football Coaches Poll?
item.description: The 2026 preseason Coaches Poll has some hits and misses in the top 25, relative to expectations in more advanaced, analytics-driven rankings systems.
item.content:encoded:
The release of the preseason Coaches Poll means one thing: college football season is almost here. And it's time to start the arguing.

That arguing this offseason has mostly centered on the fight for supremacy between the SEC and Big Ten Conferences, thanks to the Indiana Hoosiers winning the National Championship and closing out an undefeated 16-0 season. That was just a few months after Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian said undefeated teams were a thing of the past in the NIL era.

But 2026 is a new season, and thanks to the transfer portal and NIL, it's harder than ever to gauge the strength of a team or roster from year to year. This upcoming season might be even harder than most, considering the turnover among coaches at top-tier programs.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL IS FINALLY BACK AFTER MONTHS OF NCAA LAWSUITS, NIL DRAMA AND CONGRESSIONAL FIGHTS

The Florida Gators have a new head coach in Jon Sumrall. Lane Kiffin fled Ole Miss for the LSU Tigers, while Pete Golding took over in Oxford. Auburn hired Alex Golesh from USF. Penn State replaced James Franklin with Matt Campbell. Kyle Whittingham left his longtime home at Utah to run a Michigan Wolverines program beset by turmoil after the departure of Sherrone Moore. Morgan Scalley is the new head coach in Salt Lake, while UCLA brought in Bob Chesney to try and revitalize the program.

So how did the coaches, or more accurately, the staffers who actually do the voting in the poll, do in evaluating all of these changes heading into 2026?

The short answer? Not too bad, actually.

To evaluate it, we can compare it against a potentially less biased source: analytics-driven ranking systems. These polls, which rely on efficiency numbers on offense, defense, and special teams, adjusted for opponent, are often a better indication of a team's underlying quality. Though it's up to human voters to weigh the importance of wins and losses, relative to how a team played.

THREE TEAMS RANKED OUTSIDE THE TOP-12 OF THE COACHES POLL WHO WILL MAKE THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

For example, if say, LSU racks up 700 yards on offense, allows 75 yards on defense, but fumbles at the 1-yard line every drive, the Tigers would get credit for the efficiency they demonstrated on offense and defense, even if they lose 3-0. Evaluating the importance of how a team played to wins and losses is one of the most important things poll voters, and now the selection committee, can do. And they often do it poorly.

But to test these preseason rankings, we can compare it to SP+, created by Bill Connelly and housed at ESPN. One of the best of this type of metric-driven ranking systems, SP+ released its preseason "poll" ahead of the 2026 season, evaluating last year's performances, returning production, and recruiting rankings.

Impressively, the top three are almost identical. Ohio State and Oregon are the top two teams in SP+, and the top two teams in the Coaches Poll. Georgia sits third in the poll, and fourth in SP+. They're followed by Texas and Notre Dame in the poll, though the Irish are third in SP+ and Texas is just sixth.

So the top five or six teams are fairly close, implying that the poll does a good job of reflecting which teams are expected to be the strongest in 2026. Though some of the divergence towards the middle part of the poll does reflect a common, and often predictable, bias.

Oklahoma and Ole Miss, both playoff teams in 2025, sit ninth and 10th in the poll, but just 12th and 16th in SP+. And that's where the "human element" comes into play. Analytics systems weren't as high on either team as humans were in 2025. But both play in the SEC, which frequently means they're ranked higher than they should be in preseason polls. See Florida and LSU in 2025, which were 15th and ninth in the preseason AP Poll in 2025, only to finish 4-8 and 7-6 respectively. Big program names and passionate fan bases may "mean more," but they don't always translate to on-field success.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

On the other hand, a few SEC teams might feel a bit undervalued by the coaches, including, oddly enough, LSU. The Tigers are 13th in the poll, but 10th in SP+. The numbers expect big things from their big transfer portal class, especially with the quarterback quality and depth they'll have in Kiffin's first season. Tennessee, too, is a bit underrated, coming in 18th in the poll, but 15th in SP+. The Volunteers had some impressive performances last year, though weren't able to get the job done in big games. While that'll have to change to return to the playoff, they're on the bubble, quality-wise.

Another underrated team? The Texas Tech Red Raiders. Perhaps no team has utilized NIL and the portal as well as Texas Tech to rebuild its program overnight, and it worked swimmingly in 2025. Yes, the Red Raiders were shut out by Oregon in the playoff, but they are expected to have a top-10 offense, and top-11 defense. That's a pretty good combination, which is why they're seventh in SP+, but just 12th in the poll.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

The biggest miss? Houston, of all teams. The Cougars sit at No. 24 in the poll, but just 36th in SP+. That Houston-Texas Tech game in Week 3 will likely be a matchup of two "ranked" teams, but one is very different than the other.

Still, all in all, the Coaches Poll isn't as bad as it could be. Yes, there are some misses, but for the most part, teams are within a few spots of where they'd be with a more advanced form of ranking than just guessing based on 2025. And hey, for fans of those teams in the 10-20 range, remember Indiana started last season at No. 19, before going 16-0 and winning a title. That's the best part of college football, you just never know.

item.title: Smug Megan Rapinoe goes on unhinged rant, attacks Riley Gaines and Sophie Cunningham over women's sports
item.description: Megan Rapinoe attacked Sophie Cunningham on her podcast for posing with Riley Gaines, demanding ideological conformity over a single post-game photo.
item.content:encoded:
Megan Rapinoe is back, taking shots at women's sports advocates and once again insisting the differences between male and female athletes shouldn't matter in women's sports.

Speaking on her "Why Are You Like This?" podcast — a question sports fans have been asking about her for years — the former USWNT star went after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham and OutKick's own Riley Gaines after the two posed for a photo following the Fever's game against the Minnesota Lynx.

Rapinoe supports allowing biological males to compete in women's sports, yet frames women who object, and even athletes who simply stand beside them, as the villains.

MEGAN RAPINOE SAYS EFFORTS TO BAR TRANS ATHLETES FROM WOMEN'S SPORTS ARE 'ATTACK ON WOMEN IN SOCIETY'

"I want to address the controversy that is happening right now around trans women in sports," Rapinoe opened.

"As you know, I've talked about this a lot and will continue to keep talking about this."

She went straight after Cunningham, a fan-favorite WNBA guard now popular with young girls across the country.

Cunningham's big offense? Posing for a picture with Gaines, an athlete who watched female swimmers get robbed of trophies by a biological male and pledged to stop it from happening to anyone else.

In fact, when Gaines attended that game, arena security singled her out as the only person in the building forced to put down a simple sign supporting Cunningham ("Sophie thank you - a Girl Mom").

That selective censorship shows just how directly Gaines and Cunningham are running counter to the WNBA's enforced agenda.

"I don't know Sophie, so I can only project what I see about her beliefs based on her actions, and seeing a picture of her with Riley Gaines after the game told me everything I need to know about what's happening," Rapinoe scoffed.

Rapinoe then demanded ideological conformity from the WNBA star, treating a single post-game photo with Gaines as proof of Cunningham's beliefs rather than addressing anything Cunningham herself had said.

Zero facts, zero conversation. Just pure guilt by association, which is a classic Rapinoe move.

"Sophie has claimed both to love trans people and support Title IX. And this is where I think the accountability with having a major platform is extremely important."

RILEY GAINES SAYS WNBA IS 'HELLBENT' ON BEING AN ACTIVIST ORGANIZATION OVER A BASKETBALL LEAGUE

Rapinoe then turned her attention to Gaines.

"Riley Gaines has made it her life's mission to exclude trans people from public life," Rapinoe claimed.

"She's directly tied to the Heritage Foundation, the authors of Project 2025 and now 2026, who have now published a report that suggests that they want to repeal Title IX, the very piece of legislation that allowed athletes like Sophie and myself to compete in sports."

What Rapinoe conveniently forgets, or deliberately omits, is that Gaines was in the water, competing head-to-head against a MAN (Will "Lia" Thomas) at the 2022 NCAA Championships.

Activists like Rapinoe cheered for Will Thomas' inclusion in the pool and the women's locker room.

It's classic Rapinoe spin. Wipe away Gaines' actual experience in the pool, frame her as a political operative, and ignore the real damage inflicted on female sports. Rapinoe wants fans to pretend Gaines's actual experience doesn't exist while dragging Cunningham through the mud over a simple picture. Facts take a backseat in Rapinoe's world. It's not about what happened in the pool or with other female athletes who've competed against men and echoed Gaines' sentiments.

SOFTBALL HALL OF FAMER SENDS BLUNT WARNING TO THOSE DEFENDING INCLUSION OF BIOLOGICAL MALES IN FEMALE SPORTS

"You can hear it even in the language being used that the root of trans exclusion is to protect young girls from men," Rapinoe said. "To be clear, I would love to have that conversation and it's much needed in this country. But it frames the conversation as if we're protecting young girls from men being in WNBA locker rooms, not happening. It villainizes trans girls as if they're somehow magically older than their peers. Or are men, when in reality, they are also young girls. These laws are excluding kids. Kids from playing youth sports."

She dismissed concerns at elite levels, claiming, "If we want to have a conversation around elite sports, there are effective policies that have been in place for many years that no one noticed because they worked."

She finished her rant by scoffing at anyone who dares disagree. "So, if anybody is taking these talking points as legit or believing they're protecting young girls in sports? I just have to ask, are you serious?"

Yes, people are serious.

Parents, female athletes and fans are serious about protecting single-sex sports, the very purpose Title IX was created to guarantee.

Rather than grapple with why Gaines entered this debate or why Cunningham chose to stand beside her, Rapinoe portrays both women as the problem.

Unhinged Rapinoe can defend her position, but Gaines and Cunningham are standing up for female athletes and the young girls dreaming of a level playing field.

item.title: Eating too much protein could backfire, experts warn after longevity review
item.description: Excess protein may strain the body in sedentary people, but adding exercise and plant-based protein sources could unlock compounding longevity benefits.
item.content:encoded:
A recent scientific review challenged the idea that consuming more protein necessarily leads to better health, suggesting that the optimal amount depends on factors such as age, activity level and overall health.

After reviewing more than 350 studies, researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison concluded that while higher protein intake can support muscle growth and other health benefits, consuming more than the body needs may offer little advantage.

In fact, it could even reduce longevity in some sedentary adults, particularly when protein comes from certain sources or amino acid profiles, they concluded.

LIVING LONGER COULD HINGE ON ONE SURPRISING DIETARY CHANGE, STUDY REVIEW SUGGESTS

For those wondering how to adjust their own diets in light of these findings, the answer lies in personalization, activity level and food sources, according to experts.

"We are hearing conflicting things from doctors ... and influencers," Tanya Freirich, a registered dietitian nutritionist in Charlotte, North Carolina, told Fox News Digital.

"The message lately has been to increase your protein," said the expert, who was not involved in the research. 

"However, we do know that excess protein is associated with negative effects. It can put a strain on your kidney health, and it can interfere with bone and calcium homeostasis."

POPULAR SMOOTHIE INGREDIENT MAY REDUCE ONE KEY HEALTH BENEFIT, STUDY SUGGESTS

For sedentary individuals, cutting back on excess protein isn’t the only option, according to Freirich. Increasing physical activity can also help the body use nutrients more effectively.

"If you are moving your body — strength training, building muscle or doing sports — you probably do need a little bit more protein," she noted.

"Now, let's say you were a super active person and unfortunately had an injury and have gone down to a very sedentary level — you should modify your protein because your body is not utilizing it in the same way."

Exercise may also support longevity in ways that go beyond nutrition, Freirich noted, by helping people stay active and independent.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Adding exercise is always a good idea because it is associated with having fewer falls, having more joy in life and protecting you from injury," she said.

For those looking to rebalance their nutrition without doing a total overhaul, Freirich offered the following five tips.

No. 1: Focus on plate proportions: Aim for 50% of your plate to consist of vegetables, 25% protein and 25% starches or whole grains.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

No. 2: Do the quick math: A general guideline is to consume 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day for adults with lower activity levels, while those who are more physically active may benefit from about 1.0 gram per kilogram per day.

No. 3: Eat the rainbow: Incorporate fruits and vegetables across various colors to ensure a diverse intake of vitamins and micro-nutrients.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

No. 4: Switch to plant proteins: Shift a portion of animal protein toward plant-based alternatives like lentils, beans, chickpeas and seeds. "A lot of people who were on protein-restricted diets and saw better health outcomes were eating a lot of their proteins from plants," Freirich noted.

No. 5: Stick to whole foods: Unprocessed foods support natural satiety signals. "Moving away from really processed foods to more unprocessed foods actually helps your body regulate a lot better," Freirich advised.

Ultimately, dietary choices shouldn't be governed by a single headline or study, according to the expert.

"Research is ever-evolving," Freirich said. "Everyone should think about their personal situation and discuss it with healthcare providers to figure out the best route for them."

FIRST ON FOX: House Republicans are threatening the Smithsonian's federal funding amid GOP outrage over the museum system's presentation of American history.

"The Smithsonian is accountable to the taxpayers. So defunding them in certain ways, or tying their funds to requirements, I think is probably the best way to ensure that we bring the Smithsonian back to its required mandate," Rep. Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., told Fox News Digital. "And that is to tell the truth about the American story, and to tell about the exceptionalism of this country and its people."

Congress allocates roughly $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to the Smithsonian Institution every year, which oversees 21 museums and the National Zoo. It also receives private funding.

But Republicans have heaped scrutiny in recent weeks on the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, accusing its curators of long painting an overly critical and "woke" picture of the country's past while ignoring its triumphs.

TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED

Clyde, who is on the House Appropriations Committee — which is one of two panels on Capitol Hill tasked with mapping out how Congress spends part of the yearly budget — suggested that using the legislative branch's power of the purse could compel museum curators to change that.

"We can tie funding to specific requirements, and I think that might be the most effective way to go — saying that... 'You have to highlight the exceptionalism. You have highlighted the good things that [the Founding Fathers have] done. You know, there's no perfect country because there's not a perfect person. But we are the best there is on the planet Earth," Clyde said.

Another House Appropriations Committee member, Rep. Ben Cline, R-Va., told Fox News Digital, "The Smithsonian’s role is to teach historic facts, not to put our country under a political kaleidoscope of woke ideology."

WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ AFTER EXPLOSIVE HEARING

"As Congressional Appropriators, it is our duty to ensure that taxpayer dollars are being used responsibly. If the Smithsonian is unable and unwilling to have an objective view of our Nation’s history, House Republicans will have to act," Cline said.

Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, a third House appropriator, told Fox News Digital that stricter guardrails on Smithsonian funding are "justified."

"Congress has the responsibility to ensure those funds are used to celebrate and preserve Amrican history, not distort it," Cloud said.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order late last month directing Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to utilize existing avenues "to restore trust in the Smithsonian Institution," including installing "temporary exhibits or signage on [federally owned] sidewalks, walkways, and land used by the public that corrects inaccurate information presented in the Museum."

The issue came before Congress in July when Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, led a hearing where Republicans accused the National Museum of American History of promoting a politicized agenda on issues of race, class, gender and sexuality, at the expense of accurate teachings.

The Committee on House Administration, led by Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Wis., led a similar hearing scrutinizing the Smithsonian's teachings.

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

Democrats, on the other hand, have accused Republicans of trying to "whitewash" controversial moments in history while erasing the struggles and contributions of the country's minority populations.

"They want to rewrite the history of this country and take away the resources and leadership of people who have fought, marched and served this country for generations," Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., said during Gill's hearing. "We refuse to let historians, artists, scholars, and people who love these institutions with their entire hearts to be punished by an administration that is trying to exercise...political control, and rewrite American history."

The House and Senate are both working through proposals to fund the government for fiscal year (FY) 2027, which begins on Oct. 1. The House proposal would allocate roughly $961 million to the Smithsonian Institution, an 11% reduction from the current level.

But there's still a long way to go before both chambers strike a deal, with time for House conservatives to push for new guardrails or even less funding.

Fox News Digital reached out to the House Appropriations Committee for comment.

item.title: What our students learned at Auschwitz could help end hate in higher education
item.description: The RISE Leadership Initiative sent students from a historically Black university and a Jewish university to Auschwitz to confront hatred together.
item.content:encoded:
Some of the most important lessons universities can teach are not on any syllabus.

This past June, each of us sent students to Poland as part of a joint program. In a small shop in Warsaw, a Polish clerk refused to place change directly into the hand of a young Wilberforce University student. She had traveled four thousand miles to study the machinery of hatred at Auschwitz, but she did not need the field trip for bias and hatred to find her. It met her at the cash register.

What happened next is the reason the trip was organized in the first place. This young woman’s peers, consisting of Black students from the nation’s oldest private historically Black university and Jewish students from the largest university under Jewish auspices in America, closed ranks around her. For the rest of the trip, they walked as one group. They got looks. They kept walking.

THE GREAT BETRAYAL: HOW RADICAL PROGRESSIVES ARE DYNAMITING THE BLACK-JEWISH ALLIANCE

What we learned, and what we believe every university in America needs to hear, is that the answer to hatred and division on campus is not another statement, task force or training. It is to give students the opportunity to encounter obstacles and learn how to overcome them.

Students who live history together, who grieve, eat and walk through it side by side, build the kind of understanding that no seminar can teach and no demagogue can easily undo. Universities have always had the power to create those encounters. Too few choose to.

The problem we set out to address is one every campus leader recognizes. American campuses are fractured. Students increasingly sort themselves into groups that share their identity, their background and their grievances. Meanwhile, antisemitism has surged, racism persists and students of different backgrounds can pass four years on the same campus without ever truly encountering one another.

We lead two universities that, on paper, have little in common: one founded to strengthen Jewish heritage, the other founded in 1856 to educate Black Americans a decade before slavery’s end. Yet both institutions educate diverse student bodies and share a commitment to serving humanity.

BACK TO SCHOOL SHOULD NOT MEAN BACK TO FEAR FOR JEWISH STUDENTS

This summer, we brought our students together through the RISE Leadership Initiative, conceived by Jack Simony, president of the Auschwitz Jewish Center Foundation. They met first in New York, where they sat with Holocaust survivors in Brooklyn, and then in Poland. They traveled to Warsaw, where they shared a Sabbath dinner within hours of landing; to Treblinka, where none of the machinery of death remains; and to Auschwitz-Birkenau, where so much still does: 80,000 pairs of shoes, the luggage and the ashes that guides say still surface when the wind blows.

This experiment suggests a different path, and the evidence from that week speaks for itself.

On that first Friday night, our students were strangers seated at a common table: Jewish students explaining the Kiddush and the challah to peers who had never attended a Sabbath meal. Seven days later, at a final dinner in Kraków, those same students sat together in tears, unwilling to let the evening end. What happened in between was not simply a program. It was an encounter.

A young woman realized that the metal strips she had been scootering across in the sidewalk traced the walls of the Warsaw Ghetto. She had been gliding, unknowingly, in and out of a graveyard of sorts where 400,000 Jews had been forced to live in squalor within 1.3 square miles.

In Kraków, students shared lunch with a survivor, so the journey that began in the presence of living memory in Brooklyn ended in it, too. At Birkenau, walking through the barracks after the crematorium, one Wilberforce student turned to the Jewish classmates beside her and said simply, "I know this is personal to you. Now I too have seen and felt it and can bear witness."

The learning ran in both directions. Our Jewish students, who grew up with the Holocaust as a family legacy, included two grandchildren of survivors. They heard their Black peers describe a different kind of erasure: Enslaved Africans were deliberately stripped of their histories, their lineages and their very names.

One group carries the memory of everything that was lost, while the other carries the loss of memory itself. Standing together in Poland, our students understood viscerally what no seminar could teach: although their histories are different, they rhyme.

This should not be a novel idea. Black and Jewish Americans built one of the great alliances of the 20th century, marching together, organizing together and standing together in the struggle for civil rights. That alliance has frayed in recent decades, picked apart by those who profit from division. Rebuilding it will not happen through joint statements. It will happen the way it happened the first time: through shared experience, shoulder to shoulder.

To be sure, one trip does not solve campus division, and we do not pretend a few dozen students constitute a movement. But the elements that made it work — shared history, honest conversation over a meal, difficult places and time spent together — cost far less than the crisis-management apparatus universities have built instead. What is missing is not simply money. It is the willingness to build programs that foster authentic human connection.

That is why the exchange cannot run in only one direction. The next chapter will take these same students to Ghana, where they will encounter the history and legacy of the transatlantic slave trade. Jewish students who invited their classmates into the history of the Holocaust will become guests in another people’s historical memory. That reciprocity is not an addition to the model. It is central to it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

We invite our fellow presidents from Jewish institutions, historically Black colleges or universities and every university in between to build their own versions. Pair your students. Take them to the places where history happened. Let them grieve together, eat together and walk together through streets where they may be challenged together.

Because our students learned something in Warsaw that no task force will ever produce: when prejudice refused to put change into one student’s hand, every hand in the group reached out.

Dr. Vann R. Newkirk, Sr., is president of Wilberforce University, the first private historically Black college and university (HBCU) in the United States.

item.title: Debut of former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin on NBC SNF had highlight moments but was too careful and rehearsed
item.description: Mike Tomlin's NBC Sunday Night Football debut showed flashes of his signature personality but felt scripted and tame for much of the pregame broadcast.
item.content:encoded:
It took almost the entire NBC Sunday Night Football pregame show, but just before the Hall of Fame Game began, new studio analyst Mike Tomlin was asked which division he believes is the NFL's toughest.

"Yeah, that's easy," the former Pittsburgh-Steelers-coach-turned-analyst said, "I thought you had a tough one: That's the NFC West, man. It's 'The Game of Thrones' out west.

"Everyone dies."

SUPER BOWL-WINNING COACH MIKE TOMLIN LANDS NBC ROLE ON 'FOOTBALL NIGHT IN AMERICA' BROADCAST

Tomlin earlier discussed what he's expecting out of his first NFL season away from the sideline.

"I'm looking forward to going undefeated," he joked.

And with that we got a glimpse why there are such high expectations for Tomlin in his rookie season on the pregame show prior to NBC's Sunday Night Football broadcast.

In those moments, Tomlin was Tomlin. He was candid, pithy, insightful and even funny.

But to say the once dynamic coach and leader was that during the rest of this one-hour broadcast is wrong. He wasn't. He was, instead, kind of scripted.

Rehearsed.

Tame.

So, he's got some growing to do.

We have no idea if Tomlin will tell producers to spare him their stay-safe broadcasting advice and give himself time to grow and loosen up. He might decide this season's work with NBC is a one-and-done experience and return to an NFL sideline next offseason.

But for the 22 shows NBC will broadcast from September through January, the hope is Tomlin does on air what he wanted his players to do on the field:

Go to work with his hair on fire.

Let loose.

Be himself.

(Confession: I'm a Tomlin admirer. Once the youngest coach to win a Super Bowl, and having taken his Steelers to two Super Bowls, 13 postseason berths and eight AFC North titles without a losing season, I'll vote for Tomlin's induction into the Pro Football Hall of Fame some day.)

But the Sports Broadcasting Hall of Fame? Let's agree he's off to a slow start.

Weighing Tomlin's hits against his misses shows he needs to understand we don't need to hear the obvious. Because we know the obvious, like when he was discussing the trade that sent two-time defensive player of the year Myles Garrett from the Cleveland Browns to the Los Angeles Rams.

"I speak for everyone in three cities in the northeastern part of the United States [that have AFC North teams]," Tomlin said. "They're glad he went west."

Well, no kidding, coach. So, keep going.

Did Browns GM Andrew Berry make a mistake? Did he get robbed by the Rams? Who won that trade?

Coach Tomlin last year criticized Berry for trading Joe Flacco to the AFC North division rival Cincinnati Bengals and giving that team life. But analyst Tomlin didn't go anywhere near giving us his feelings about this trade.

At halftime, the analysts discussed the matchup between the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots to open the regular season on Sept. 9, a game NBC will broadcast.

Tomlin offered this: "When the games start, winning matters ..."

Got it. Thanks.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Look, the NBC pregame show is maybe 90 percent entertainment and 10 percent journalism.

They talked about Bill Belichick not being among the Hall of Fame Class that will be enshrined on Saturday and mentioned all his accomplishments, of which there are many, including a record six Super Bowl victories as the head coach.

But they didn't mention Spygate, which was a major reason Belichick did not make it on his first ballot.

And since entertainment is the emphasis, Tomlin will shine once/if he loosens up because he has as colorful a way of expressing himself as anyone on the planet. Will he do that and convince us he knows what he's doing as an analyst like he did when he was a coach?

"Ask me in about six months," Tomlin told Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth in a rare unscripted moment of candor.

item.title: Church protesters could face tougher penalties under rare bipartisan crackdown
item.description: A bipartisan House bill would impose civil fines up to $10,000 for protests that disrupt worship within 100 feet of a house of worship entrance.
item.content:encoded:
There's a rare show of bipartisan unity in the House of Representatives this week, as lawmakers from opposite sides of the aisle come together to crack down on destructive protests targeting houses of worship.

Reps. Brad Knott, R-N.C., and Tom Suozzi, D-N.Y., are introducing a bill to make it a crime to knowingly disrupt or impede people from attending a religious service.

That includes demonstrations taking place within 100 feet "from any pedestrian or vehicular entryway of any house of worship, during the period beginning 1 hour before the start of and ending 1 hour after the conclusion of a scheduled religious service," according to legislative text obtained by Fox News Digital.

VIDEO SHOWS MOB OF TEENS INVADING NYC CHURCH OF SCIENTOLOGY IN SOCIAL MEDIA STUNT

A violation of those guidelines would carry a $2,500 civil fine on the first offense, a $5,000 penalty on the second offense, and $10,000 for a third.

The bill does carve out limitations, however, such as demonstrations that are taking place with a federal, state, or local government-issued permit.

The text's language also specifically classifies disruptions based on things like volume, duration, and impact, rather than the content of speech — meaning the First Amendment is still protected.

"Today, many Americans are unable to worship without fear of harassment, assault, or other forms of intimidation. The right to worship freely is foundational to our nation and was one of the motivations for its founding. No American should ever feel that their choice is between worshiping in fear and not worshiping at all," Knott said.

FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP DOJ REACHES SETTLEMENT WITH PRO-LIFE PROTESTER TARGETED BY BIDEN ADMIN

Suozzi said he supports people's right to peacefully protest but "attendees of religious services should not be harassed, threatened, intimidated, or targeted for practicing their faith."

At least four states adopted laws banning the disruption of religious services earlier this year, the Associated Press reported.

It followed an incident in which Minnesota demonstrators upended service at a church where a federal immigration official was reportedly a pastor.
